## Biography

I am a Ph.D. candidate in the Department of Economics at the University of California, Davis. **I will be on the 2026-2027 academic job market.**

My research lies at the intersection of international economics, macroeconomics, and geoeconomics. I study how geopolitical risk affects firms' access to finance and how the resulting financing disruptions reshape their invoicing decisions and the pattern of currency use across countries.

My job market paper examines how U.S. financial sanctions against Chinese entities shape invoicing currency choice in trade. I find that the increase in sanctions is associated with relatively greater use of the renminbi and less use of the dollar in countries that relied more on imports from China. I develop a model showing how the risk of restrictions on dollar-linked credit can encourage firms to switch currencies, even when borrowing rates remain unchanged. The paper highlights the reliability of working capital finance as a channel through which financial sanctions can make the dollar less attractive for international trade.

My applied microeconomic research uses detailed retail scanner and household purchase data to study firms’ and consumers’ responses to taxes and health risks. One project examines how retailers' pricing and promotional responses to local sugar-sweetened beverage taxes vary with the characteristics of the consumers they serve. Another studies soda purchases around households' first purchases of diabetes-monitoring products, a potential marker of heightened health awareness. I find a modest but immediate decline in soda purchases, followed by little further adjustment. Together, these projects provide microeconomic evidence to inform habit-based models of consumer demand and firm pricing, with the broader goal of understanding price rigidity in macroeconomics.
